title: Extreme Humid Heat Cuts Brain Blood Flow by a Third and Forces the Heart Into Overdrive — Here's What That Means for You
excerpt: A scientific simulation reveals how quickly high humidity overwhelms the body's defences, with particular risks for South Asians carrying undiagnosed hypertension and prediabetes
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Extreme humid heat reduces brain blood flow by 33%, risking cognitive function.
  • The heart works 30% harder in high humidity, increasing cardiac strain.
  • South Asians face higher risks due to prevalent undiagnosed hypertension and prediabetes.
  • Heat indices exceeded 110°F in major cities with large South Asian populations.
  • CDC recommends hydration and air conditioning to combat extreme heat effects.

University of South Wales study
As half of America swelters through one of the most punishing early-July heat waves in recent memory, a scientific simulation from the University of South Wales has put hard numbers on what extreme humid heat does to the human body — and the findings should worry anyone who assumes they can simply tough it out. Researchers placed volunteers inside an environmental chamber cranked to 40°C (104°F) and systematically measured blood flow, brain function, and cardiac output. At a dry 20 percent humidity, the body coped largely as expected: sweating kicked in, core temperature rose gradually, and cognitive function held. But when scientists dialled humidity up to 85 percent — replicating the damp, sauna-like conditions that are becoming increasingly common in the American South and Midwest — the body's defences collapsed with startling speed. ## Your Brain Loses a Third of Its Blood Supply The most alarming finding was neurological. Blood flow to the brain plummeted from a baseline of 600 millilitres per minute to just 400 — a 33 percent drop. That is not a subtle dip. It means the brain is being starved of oxygen and glucose at precisely the moment it needs to make sharp decisions about safety: when to stop working, when to seek shade, when to call for help. "For older patients or individuals with pre-existing conditions, this dual cardiovascular and neurological toll is a massive, life-threatening deal," the researchers noted. Under sustained humid heat, some volunteers were physically unable to complete basic tasks like standing up from a chair. ## The Heart Works 30 Percent Harder — for Nothing > **""For older patients or individuals with pre-existing conditions, this dual cardiovascular and neurological toll is a massive, life-threatening deal," the researchers noted."** Simultaneously, the heart was forced to pump roughly 30 percent harder to compensate for blood pooling near the skin's surface as the body desperately tried to radiate heat. Internal blood pressure spiked even during minimal physical exertion. For someone with undiagnosed hypertension or early-stage heart disease — conditions that are disproportionately common among South Asians — this invisible cardiac strain could tip the balance from discomfort to emergency. The simulation confirmed what emergency physicians have long suspected: humid heat is far more dangerous than dry heat at the same temperature. When humidity is high, sweat cannot evaporate efficiently, stripping the body of its primary cooling mechanism and trapping heat internally. ![American South — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Andrew_Jackson_monument%2C_New_Orleans%2C_USA.jpg/3840px-Andrew_Jackson_monument%2C_New_Orleans%2C_USA.jpg) ## Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora The timing is significant. The U.S. heat wave that scorched Fourth of July celebrations across the eastern seaboard and Sun Belt saw heat indices exceeding 110°F in cities with large South Asian populations — Houston, Dallas, Atlanta, Phoenix, and the Tri-State area. The National Weather Service issued excessive heat warnings covering nearly half the country.
Health Risks for South Asians
›Higher rates of hypertension and prediabetes among Indian Americans.
›Conditions often develop by mid-40s, frequently without symptoms.
›Elderly and dementia patients are especially vulnerable.
›Urgent message for families with elderly relatives.
South Asians in the U.S. face a compound risk. Research from Northwestern University's MASALA study has shown that Indian Americans develop hypertension and prediabetes at significantly higher rates than other groups — often by their mid-40s, and often without symptoms. These are precisely the conditions that make humid-heat exposure most dangerous, because the cardiovascular system is already operating closer to its limits. For NRI families with elderly parents — whether in the U.S. or in India, which endured its own record-breaking pre-monsoon heat this spring — the message is urgent. Dementia patients are especially vulnerable because their bodies lose the ability to sense and react to temperature changes, and they may not be able to communicate distress. ## What the Science Says You Should Actually Do The CDC's recommendations sound simple but are non-negotiable in extreme heat: drink 8 ounces of water every 15 to 20 minutes during outdoor activity, but not more than 48 ounces per hour (overhydration depletes essential electrolytes). Stay in air-conditioned spaces during peak hours. And critically, recognise that warm overnight temperatures — which are becoming the new normal in many U.S. cities — prevent the body from recovering, compounding risk day after day. Dr. Hiba Khan of the Cleveland Clinic offers practical advice for families caring for older relatives: flavoured water or high-water-content fruits like watermelon can help with hydration when plain water is refused, and sun-protective clothing is essential because sweating patterns change with age and cognitive decline. The University of South Wales simulation delivered its most important message in data, not words: by the time you feel the heat is "tough," your brain has already lost a third of its fuel and your heart is sprinting. In a warming world where humid heat waves are growing more frequent and more intense, that knowledge is no longer academic — it is survival information. *Sources: University of South Wales environmental chamber study; NBC Palm Springs; CDC heat safety guidelines; Cleveland Clinic; USA Today; Northwestern MASALA study*
